title: Chapter 1 Drill: Perioperative Medicine, Anesthesia, and Pharmacology

items.stem: A 70-year-old man takes apixaban for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 3 and normal renal function. He is scheduled for an elective low anterior resection, a high-bleeding-risk operation. How should apixaban be managed?
options: Stop it two days before surgery and omit bridging anticoagulation
Stop it five days before surgery and bridge with injectable therapy
Continue it through the morning of surgery to prevent a stroke
Stop it the evening before and restart on the same night
items.explanation: For high-bleeding-risk procedures in patients with normal renal function, direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban are usually held for about two days, which allows sufficiently low drug levels for surgery and neuraxial anesthesia. Bridging is not needed because of their predictable, short offset and has been shown to increase bleeding without lowering thromboembolism. Continuing the drug or holding it only one night risks major surgical and neuraxial bleeding.

items.stem: Ten minutes after a spinal anesthetic for a transurethral procedure, a 66-year-old man has a blood pressure of 78/44 mm Hg and a heart rate of 48 beats per minute. He is warm and alert, with a block level at the nipple line. Which is the best next intervention?
options: Immediate intubation for presumed total spinal anesthesia
Intravenous ephedrine, with fluid and a position that supports venous return
A large dose of intravenous beta blocker for presumed supraventricular tachyarrhythmia
Cardioversion for the bradycardia and low pressure
items.explanation: A high sympathetic block from neuraxial anesthesia produces vasodilation and, when the cardiac accelerator fibers are blocked, bradycardia. Treatment is a vasopressor with chronotropic effect such as ephedrine, plus fluids and positioning. Because the patient remains alert and ventilating, total spinal anesthesia is not present. A beta blocker would worsen bradycardia, and cardioversion is unnecessary because there is no tachyarrhythmia or unstable rhythm requiring it.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with controlled hypertension is scheduled for an elective open nephrectomy. She has no cardiac symptoms. She walks a mile on level ground at a steady pace, climbs a flight of stairs without stopping, and does her own housework. How does this history affect her preoperative cardiac evaluation?
options: Her age alone requires a pharmacologic stress test before any major operation proceeds
Any major abdominal operation requires coronary angiography first
She exceeds four metabolic equivalents, so she proceeds without stress testing
Functional capacity counts only after a formal treadmill test
items.explanation: Good functional capacity, meaning the ability to climb a flight of stairs or walk briskly, corresponds to at least four metabolic equivalents and predicts low perioperative cardiac risk. In a patient without active cardiac conditions, further testing would not change management. Age by itself is not an indication for stress testing, angiography is reserved for patients whose symptoms or results would justify revascularization anyway, and a self-reported activity history is an accepted measure of capacity.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with prior coronary stenting takes atorvastatin and is scheduled for an elective open sigmoid resection next week. His surgeon asks whether to hold the statin because of concerns about muscle injury under anesthesia. What is the best advice?
options: Hold it from one week before surgery until discharge
Continue the statin throughout the perioperative period without interruption
Switch to a different cholesterol agent on the day of surgery to avoid muscle injury
Stop it only if the creatine kinase is mildly elevated
items.explanation: Statins should be continued through surgery in patients already taking them, and should be started in many patients with vascular disease or elevated risk. Withdrawal has been associated with more perioperative cardiac events through loss of plaque-stabilizing effects. Concern for myopathy is unfounded in asymptomatic patients, and a routine creatine kinase is not needed. Substituting another agent offers no advantage and interrupts proven therapy.

items.stem: On the fifth day after a colectomy, a 64-year-old man develops a temperature of 39 degrees C. His abdomen is soft and nontender, the wound is clean, and he is eating. He has a central venous catheter placed for parenteral nutrition, and the insertion site is red with purulent drainage. What is the best management?
options: Cultures from the catheter and a peripheral vein, then remove the line
Continue the catheter and give an antipyretic only
Exchange the catheter over a guidewire and keep using the same insertion site
Obtain CT of the abdomen before any other evaluation
items.explanation: Fever with purulence at a central line site suggests catheter-related infection, and the source should be removed with paired cultures drawn to confirm. Guidewire exchange is inappropriate with a visibly infected site because it seeds the new catheter. Treating the fever alone ignores the source and risks bloodstream infection. Imaging is not the first step when the abdomen and wound are normal and an obvious source exists.

items.stem: A surgeon prepares to infiltrate lidocaine without epinephrine for excision of several lesions in a 70 kg man. Which of the following limits the maximum safe dose of plain lidocaine for infiltration?
options: About 12 mg per kilogram, whether or not epinephrine is added to the solution
About 1 mg per kilogram, which cannot be raised with epinephrine
About 20 mg per kilogram, because lidocaine has low toxicity
About 4.5 mg per kilogram, with a higher limit when epinephrine is added
items.explanation: The commonly cited maximum infiltration dose of plain lidocaine is about 4.5 mg per kilogram, and with epinephrine it is raised to about 7 mg per kilogram because vasoconstriction slows systemic absorption. Higher doses risk perioral numbness, seizure, and cardiovascular collapse. One percent solution contains 10 mg per milliliter, so counting the volume prevents inadvertent overdose. The other values are either far too high or needlessly restrictive.

items.stem: A surgeon is closing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed with an umbilical 12 mm port in a 48-year-old woman with obesity. What step best reduces the risk of a port-site hernia?
options: Close only the skin since the fascia heals on its own
Close the fascia at the 12 mm port site with sutures
Leave the port site open to prevent fluid collection
Use fibrin sealant over the skin instead of sutures
items.explanation: Port-site hernias occur predominantly at sites of 10 mm or larger, especially at the umbilicus, and fascial closure markedly lowers the rate. Skin closure alone leaves the defect unsupported, and leaving it open or sealing the skin does not secure the fascia. Risk factors include obesity, wound infection, and port enlargement during specimen extraction. Smaller 5 mm sites rarely need fascial closure.

items.stem: An 81-year-old woman who lives alone is scheduled for elective pancreatic resection. Her daughter notes that she has become forgetful with bills and medications. The surgical team wants a quick preoperative assessment that will help predict postoperative delirium. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: No testing, because cognitive impairment does not change surgical risk or outcomes
A full neuropsychological battery that delays surgery by months
A brief cognitive screen such as the Mini-Cog, documented before surgery
Cranial imaging for every older patient before major surgery
items.explanation: Baseline cognitive impairment is a strong risk factor for postoperative delirium and prolonged recovery, and a brief screen such as the Mini-Cog takes a few minutes. A documented baseline lets the team recognize change, tailor delirium prevention, and counsel the family. Neuropsychological testing is unnecessary for surgical planning, and routine imaging has no role without focal findings. Ignoring memory complaints misses a modifiable, high-yield risk.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with healthy lungs and heart undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy with carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum at 15 mm Hg in reverse Trendelenburg position. Which hemodynamic changes are most expected during insufflation?
options: Increased venous return from abdominal compression with a fall in systemic vascular resistance
Unchanged preload with a marked increase in cardiac output
Reduced systemic vascular resistance with increased heart rate only
Reduced venous return and cardiac output with higher systemic vascular resistance
items.explanation: Intra-abdominal pressure compresses the inferior vena cava and reduces venous return, while neurohormonal responses and mechanical compression raise systemic vascular resistance, so cardiac output tends to fall, especially with the head-up position and hypovolemia. Carbon dioxide absorption also raises arterial carbon dioxide and can cause acidosis, requiring ventilator adjustment. Healthy patients tolerate this, but those with heart disease may not, and lower insufflation pressures are safer.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease on regular hemodialysis, otherwise well and active, will have an arteriovenous fistula revision. How is his preoperative physical status best classified?
options: ASA class III, because of a severe but stable systemic disease
ASA class I, because he is active and has no symptoms
ASA class II, because he has mild controlled disease
ASA class IV, because his disease is a constant threat to his life
items.explanation: The American Society of Anesthesiologists classification grades systemic disease: class II is mild, class III is severe systemic disease with functional limitation, and class IV is a constant threat to life. End-stage renal disease on regular dialysis is a standard example of class III. A healthy patient is class I. Class IV applies to conditions such as recent myocardial infarction or sepsis with ongoing organ dysfunction, which are not present here.

items.stem: A 72-year-old unmarried man is unconscious after a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm and needs emergency repair. He has no written directive. His adult son and his longtime partner are both present and disagree on whether to proceed. How should the team obtain consent?
options: Delay the operation until the family agrees unanimously
Proceed with emergency surgery under implied consent, while locating the legal surrogate
Obtain a court order before any surgical intervention
Defer to whichever relative arrived first at the hospital
items.explanation: When a patient lacks capacity and delay would risk life, consent is implied for necessary emergency treatment that a reasonable person would accept. The team simultaneously identifies the legally recognized surrogate under local law, or an agent the patient designated, and informs them. Waiting for unanimity or a court order endangers life, and arrival order has no legal weight in choosing a surrogate.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator needs an open ventral hernia repair below the umbilicus. The surgeon plans to use electrocautery. Which approach best protects the patient and the device?
options: Use continuous monopolar cautery with the return pad on the shoulder
Avoid any electrosurgery and use sharp dissection only
Use short bursts or bipolar energy, with the return pad placed so current avoids the device
Place the return pad directly over the device pocket
items.explanation: Electromagnetic interference from monopolar cautery can be sensed as an arrhythmia and trigger inappropriate shocks. For an operation below the umbilicus, interference is less likely, but the safest approach uses bipolar energy or short monopolar bursts, with a return pad positioned so the current path does not cross the device, and a plan for tachytherapy suspension. Sharp dissection only is impractical, and pad placement near the device invites interference.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man with obesity, loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep, and hypertension will undergo an open ventral hernia repair under general anesthesia. He has never had a sleep study. He is expected to need opioid analgesia afterward. Which plan best reduces his postoperative respiratory risk?
options: Treat as probable sleep apnea with opioid-sparing analgesia and continuous pulse oximetry
Cancel the operation until a full sleep study is completed
Give long-acting opioids on a fixed schedule for comfort
Plan routine ward care since he has no diagnosed disease
items.explanation: A screening score such as STOP-Bang that suggests obstructive sleep apnea is enough to start precautions without delaying urgent or necessary surgery. Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, head-up positioning, and continuous oximetry address the main danger of postoperative airway collapse and respiratory depression. Scheduled long-acting opioids and sedatives increase that risk, and ignoring the screen leaves a preventable hazard. Cancellation is reserved for unoptimized comorbid disease, not undiagnosed snoring.

items.stem: Eight hours after an open inguinal hernia repair under spinal anesthesia, a 76-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has lower abdominal discomfort and has not voided. He is restless, and the suprapubic area is dull to percussion. What is the best next step?
options: Give a large intravenous fluid bolus to stimulate urine output and relieve the discomfort
Obtain emergency CT of the abdomen for a suspected bleed
Start an alpha agonist to improve bladder emptying
Bladder scan, then straight catheterization if the retained volume is large
items.explanation: Postoperative urinary retention is common after spinal anesthesia, pelvic or hernia surgery, and in older men with prostatic enlargement. A bladder scan confirms retention, and catheterization relieves it and avoids overdistension injury. A fluid bolus fills the bladder further, CT is not needed for a clear mechanical explanation, and alpha agonists tighten the sphincter and worsen retention. An alpha blocker might be started afterward.

items.stem: Two days after laparoscopic removal of a cortisol-secreting right adrenal adenoma, a 45-year-old woman has weakness, nausea, a blood pressure of 78/44 mm Hg, sodium of 129 mEq/L, and glucose of 58 mg/dL. She received no steroid replacement. What is the most likely cause?
options: Adrenal insufficiency from suppression of the remaining adrenal gland
Pulmonary embolism from prolonged pneumoperitoneum and reverse Trendelenburg positioning
Pheochromocytoma crisis from tumor manipulation
Acute cholecystitis causing sepsis and hypotension
items.explanation: Long-standing autonomous cortisol excess suppresses the pituitary and the contralateral adrenal gland, so after the adenoma is removed the patient is functionally adrenal insufficient. Hypotension, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, and nausea are typical. Treatment is stress-dose hydrocortisone, then tapering replacement until the axis recovers. Pheochromocytoma crisis causes hypertension, and the other diagnoses do not explain the electrolyte and glucose pattern.

items.stem: Six hours after removal of an epidural catheter, a 69-year-old woman who takes apixaban reports new severe lumbar pain and progressive leg weakness with urinary retention. Her wound is clean and afebrile. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Treat as postoperative back strain with analgesics and observe overnight
Obtain urgent spinal magnetic resonance imaging and neurosurgical consultation for decompression
Place an epidural blood patch for a presumed headache
Start high-dose antibiotics for presumed epidural abscess
items.explanation: New back pain with progressive motor deficit after neuraxial catheter removal in an anticoagulated patient indicates a spinal epidural hematoma until proved otherwise. Outcome depends on decompression within roughly the first hours of symptoms, so urgent imaging and neurosurgical involvement are required. Observation allows irreversible cord injury. A blood patch treats dural puncture headache, and an abscess is unlikely at six hours without fever.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman is receiving morphine by patient-controlled analgesia after a Whipple procedure. A nurse finds her difficult to rouse, with a respiratory rate of 6 per minute, oxygen saturation of 86 percent, and pinpoint pupils. After stopping the pump and giving oxygen, what is the next action?
options: Give a single large bolus of naloxone to fully and immediately reverse analgesia
Observe for an hour, since the effect will resolve soon
Give small incremental doses of naloxone while supporting ventilation
Give flumazenil to reverse the sedation
items.explanation: Sedation, respiratory depression, and miosis indicate opioid toxicity. After stopping the opioid, small titrated doses of naloxone restore breathing while preserving some analgesia and avoiding abrupt withdrawal, pain, and pulmonary edema. Naloxone has a shorter duration than many opioids, so monitoring continues after reversal. Waiting risks hypoxic arrest, and flumazenil antagonizes benzodiazepines, not opioids. Review of the regimen should favor multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia.

items.stem: A 77-year-old man with a perforated ulcer arrives in the operating room with a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg and a heart rate of 120. Which induction agent is most likely to preserve his hemodynamics?
options: Propofol as a standard full induction bolus given rapidly by hand
A high-dose volatile agent given by mask for a gentle inhalational induction
Midazolam as a large rapid bolus to blunt the stress response in shock
Etomidate at a reduced dose with vasopressor support ready
items.explanation: Etomidate causes minimal sympathetic suppression and little cardiovascular depression, making it a common choice in the hypovolemic or septic patient. Propofol causes vasodilation and myocardial depression, and a standard dose can produce collapse in a patient already in shock. High-dose volatile agents also lower vascular tone, and a rapid midazolam bolus is unpredictable. The drawback of etomidate is transient adrenal suppression, which matters little for a single dose.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man weighing 85 kg receives 2 g of cefazolin before incision for a prolonged open pancreatic resection. The operation continues, and four and a half hours after the dose the surgeon is still working with moderate blood loss. What is the appropriate prophylaxis step?
options: No further dose, because one preoperative dose covers the entire operation
Switch to a broader agent for the remainder of the case
Give a second dose of cefazolin, since the dosing interval has elapsed
Continue antibiotics for three days after the operation
items.explanation: Prophylactic antibiotics should be redosed at an interval of about two half-lives, which is roughly four hours for cefazolin, or after major blood loss, so tissue concentrations stay above the inhibitory level for the entire operation. A single dose is inadequate for long cases. Broadening the spectrum is unnecessary, and extending prophylaxis for days after closure adds resistance and Clostridioides difficile risk without reducing infection.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man with unresectable pancreatic cancer, severe weight loss, and a performance status of 3 asks his surgeon about hospice. He is declining chemotherapy and wishes to remain at home. Which statement about hospice eligibility is correct?
options: Hospice requires that he first complete a trial of chemotherapy
Hospice is limited to patients with a prognosis of days only
Hospice excludes patients who have previously had an operation
He may be eligible if a physician certifies a prognosis of six months or less if the disease runs its usual course
items.explanation: Hospice care is appropriate when a physician certifies a prognosis of about six months or less if the illness follows its expected course, and it emphasizes comfort, symptom control, and family support. Patients are not required to try disease-directed therapy first, and eligibility is not limited to the last days of life or affected by prior surgery. Early referral improves symptom outcomes and may reduce unwanted hospitalizations.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man had an emergency laparotomy for mesenteric ischemia. His baseline creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL. On the second postoperative day it is 1.3 mg/dL with a urine output of 0.6 mL per kilogram per hour. Which statement about this finding is correct?
options: It meets the KDIGO criterion for acute kidney injury, an increase of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours
It does not qualify until creatinine doubles from baseline
It qualifies only if urine output stays below 0.1 mL per kilogram
It is normal and requires no further evaluation
items.explanation: The KDIGO definition of acute kidney injury includes a creatinine rise of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, a rise to 1.5 times baseline within seven days, or urine output below 0.5 mL per kilogram per hour for six hours. A doubling corresponds to a higher stage, not the threshold. Even small rises predict worse outcomes, so volume status, nephrotoxins, and hemodynamics should be reviewed promptly.

items.stem: A 34-year-old nonsmoking woman with a history of severe motion sickness and nausea after previous anesthesia is scheduled for laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anesthesia. Which strategy best lowers her risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting?
options: A single dose of ondansetron given only once nausea and vomiting have begun in recovery
Combination prophylaxis with agents of different classes and opioid-sparing analgesia
Strictly avoiding any antiemetic to prevent adverse effects
Prolonged fasting to guarantee an empty stomach
items.explanation: Female sex, nonsmoking status, prior nausea or motion sickness, and postoperative opioids are the main predictors in the Apfel score, and her risk is high. Guidelines recommend two or more prophylactic agents from different classes, such as a serotonin antagonist with dexamethasone, along with propofol-based anesthesia and opioid-sparing analgesia. Treating only after symptoms start is less effective, withholding prophylaxis is inappropriate at high risk, and longer fasting does not prevent nausea.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman is scheduled for elective open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. Her only comorbidity is mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and she has quit smoking. The anesthesiologist asks which part of her risk profile is the largest modifiable contributor to postoperative pulmonary complications. What is the best answer?
options: The operative site, since upper abdominal and aortic surgery carry the highest pulmonary risk
Her sex, since women have the highest pulmonary complication rate
Her normal body mass index, which raises atelectasis risk
The use of a regional block, which raises respiratory failure
items.explanation: Surgical site is among the strongest predictors of pulmonary complications: upper abdominal, thoracic, and aortic procedures impair diaphragmatic function and cough most. Planning can reduce harm through lung expansion maneuvers, early mobilization, and regional analgesia. Female sex and a normal weight are not risk factors, and regional analgesia generally lowers pulmonary risk by improving cough and deep breathing rather than raising it.

items.stem: At the end of an operation in which rocuronium was used, a 55-year-old woman has a train-of-four count of two twitches. The anesthesiologist selects sugammadex for reversal. By what mechanism does this drug act?
options: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase and raises acetylcholine at the junction
It encapsulates free rocuronium molecules and removes them from the neuromuscular junction
It blocks muscarinic receptors to prevent bradycardia and secretions
It competes with rocuronium at the nicotinic receptor binding site
items.explanation: Sugammadex is a modified cyclodextrin that binds steroidal neuromuscular blockers such as rocuronium and vecuronium one to one, forming a complex that is excreted renally and rapidly lowering free drug at the junction. Neostigmine instead inhibits acetylcholinesterase and requires an antimuscarinic to prevent bradycardia. Sugammadex does not act at the receptor and is not effective against benzylisoquinolinium agents or succinylcholine.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man takes lisinopril for hypertension and will undergo an elective inguinal hernia repair under general anesthesia tomorrow morning. His pressure today is 128/78 mm Hg and he has no heart failure. What is the usual recommendation for the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor?
options: Take a double dose to protect against postoperative hypertension
Stop it for two full weeks beforehand to allow renin and blood pressure to recover
Take it with a sip of water on the morning of surgery
Omit it for about 24 hours before surgery to reduce intraoperative hypotension
items.explanation: When used for hypertension, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and receptor blockers are commonly held for about a day before surgery because they are associated with refractory vasoplegic hypotension under anesthesia. A two-week hold is excessive and risks rebound hypertension, and doubling the dose is dangerous. Taking the usual morning dose increases the chance of hypotension. The drug is restarted once the patient is euvolemic and hemodynamically stable.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a mechanical mitral valve and atrial fibrillation and takes warfarin with an international normalized ratio goal of 3. She needs an elective hysterectomy. Which management is most appropriate for her anticoagulation?
options: Stop warfarin about five days before surgery without bridging
Continue warfarin and give vitamin K on the morning of surgery
Stop warfarin about five days before surgery and bridge with a short-acting parenteral agent
Stop warfarin the night before surgery and restart in one month
items.explanation: A mechanical mitral valve with atrial fibrillation places the patient in the highest thromboembolic risk group, so bridging is recommended when warfarin is interrupted. Warfarin is stopped about five days ahead to allow the international normalized ratio to fall, then a short-acting parenteral anticoagulant covers the gap until after surgery. Omitting bridging risks valve thrombosis and stroke. Giving vitamin K to a continued dose is illogical, and a month-long restart delay is unsafe.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman reports a childhood itchy skin rash after amoxicillin and has had no breathing difficulty or swelling since. She will have an elective laparoscopic hernia repair with mesh. Which prophylactic choice is most appropriate?
options: Cefazolin, since her remote mild reaction does not preclude it
Vancomycin alone, since any penicillin history bars all beta-lactams
Clindamycin alone, since it is the preferred agent for hernia surgery
No prophylaxis, since she reports a drug allergy
items.explanation: Cefazolin has a side chain that differs from penicillins, and cross-reactivity is low, so it can be used in patients with a remote, non-severe reaction such as a rash. Reserving vancomycin or clindamycin for such patients leads to inferior prophylaxis and more surgical site infection. Omitting prophylaxis fails to protect a patient receiving mesh. Only a history of severe immediate reaction, such as anaphylaxis, warrants alternative agents.

items.stem: A frailty screen is added to the preoperative visit for a 78-year-old man scheduled for colectomy. He has lost weight unintentionally, walks slowly, reports exhaustion, and scores low on grip strength. How should the surgeon use this result?
options: As a firm contraindication to any operation in a patient over 75
As a predictor of complications, to guide counseling and prehabilitation planning
As unrelated to outcomes once the chronologic age is known
As a reason to skip any discussion of postoperative functional decline with the family
items.explanation: Frailty reflects diminished physiologic reserve and independently predicts postoperative complications, prolonged stay, loss of independence, and mortality beyond chronologic age. It informs shared decision-making, nutrition, exercise prehabilitation, and discharge planning rather than automatically forbidding surgery. It should open conversations about expected functional recovery, not close them. Age alone does not define risk, which is why standard tools such as the clinical frailty scale are used.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman with a prior ischemic stroke from carotid disease takes aspirin daily as secondary prevention. She will have an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She asks whether to stop the aspirin a week before to prevent bleeding. What is the best recommendation?
options: Stop aspirin for seven days, since bleeding is the main danger
Stop aspirin and substitute a short-acting anticoagulant
Continue aspirin, since the thrombotic risk outweighs the minor bleeding risk
Continue aspirin only if she has a coronary stent as well
items.explanation: In patients with established vascular disease, aspirin for secondary prevention is generally continued through procedures with modest bleeding risk, because withdrawal can precipitate stroke or myocardial infarction. The bleeding cost of continuing is small in laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Substituting an anticoagulant adds bleeding risk without equivalent benefit. The indication is secondary prevention of cerebrovascular disease, which stands on its own and does not require a stent.

items.stem: During a laparoscopic sigmoid resection, a 61-year-old man develops uncontrolled bleeding from the inferior mesenteric artery pedicle. The surgeon cannot control it with graspers or clips and the view is obscured. What is the appropriate decision?
options: Continue laparoscopically until the bleeding stops spontaneously
Increase the insufflation pressure to tamponade the vessel
Pack the abdomen and close without further dissection
Convert to an open procedure promptly to control the hemorrhage
items.explanation: Conversion to open surgery is a sign of sound judgment, not failure, when bleeding cannot be controlled, anatomy cannot be safely identified, or an injury requires repair that cannot be done laparoscopically. Delay increases blood loss and morbidity. Raising the insufflation pressure can reduce venous bleeding only slightly, causes physiologic harm, and does not control arterial bleeding. Closing without definitive control leaves an unresolved hemorrhage.

items.stem: An 83-year-old woman is recovering from hip surgery, and the resident is asked to order something for sleep. Which medication should be avoided because it raises the risk of delirium in older adults?
options: Diphenhydramine, a strongly anticholinergic sedating antihistamine
Melatonin at a low dose in the evening
Acetaminophen for pain relief at night
Scheduled early mobilization and light exposure during the daytime hours
items.explanation: Anticholinergic drugs such as diphenhydramine, along with benzodiazepines and sedative hypnotics, are on the list of potentially inappropriate medications for older adults because they precipitate confusion, urinary retention, and falls. Sleep hygiene, daytime activity, pain control with acetaminophen, and low-dose melatonin are reasonable nonpharmacologic or low-risk strategies. Medication review is a central component of multicomponent delirium prevention.

items.stem: During a rapid infusion of vancomycin before a soft tissue debridement, a 60-year-old man develops flushing of the face and upper trunk with itching. His blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg, and he has no wheeze or airway swelling. What is the best response?
options: Treat as anaphylaxis with intramuscular epinephrine
Permanently list vancomycin as an allergen and avoid it
Switch to an oral antibiotic and cancel surgery
Slow the infusion rate and give an antihistamine
items.explanation: Flushing and pruritus during rapid vancomycin infusion reflect direct histamine release, the infusion reaction once called red man syndrome, not an immunoglobulin E mediated allergy. It resolves with slowing the infusion and giving antihistamines, and the drug can be reused with a slower rate. Anaphylaxis requires airway, respiratory, or circulatory involvement. Labeling the patient allergic removes a useful agent unnecessarily, and cancelling surgery is excessive.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with a healthy body mass index is scheduled for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy at 1 pm. She asks when she may stop taking fluids. She has no diabetes, reflux, or gastroparesis. Which fasting plan matches current guidance?
options: Nothing by mouth from midnight, including water and clear liquids
Clear liquids until two hours before anesthesia, and a light meal until six hours before
Clear liquids only until twelve hours before anesthesia
Any meal until one hour before, since solids empty quickly
items.explanation: Current anesthesia guidance allows clear liquids until two hours before elective anesthesia and a light meal until six hours before, because prolonged fasting causes dehydration, discomfort, and insulin resistance without lowering aspiration risk. A midnight cutoff is outdated and unnecessarily harsh. Solids need much longer than one hour to clear the stomach, and a twelve-hour clear liquid fast gives no benefit over two hours.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man with a 40 percent total body surface area flame burn from nine days ago returns to the operating room for grafting. The anesthesiologist plans rapid-sequence induction. Which neuromuscular blocking agent should be avoided, and why?
options: Rocuronium, because it causes direct myocardial depression and arrhythmia after major burns
Vecuronium, because burn patients become resistant to its effect
Succinylcholine, because upregulated receptors can cause life-threatening hyperkalemia
Cisatracurium, because it is cleared by an organ that fails in burns
items.explanation: After major burns, immobilization, or denervation injury, extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors proliferate, and succinylcholine depolarizes them, releasing potassium and risking cardiac arrest, starting after the first day and lasting for months. Rocuronium is a safe alternative for rapid induction. Burn patients are resistant to nondepolarizing agents and need higher doses, but this is a dosing matter rather than a contraindication, and cisatracurium undergoes organ-independent degradation.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man on hemodialysis three times weekly needs an urgent but not emergent cholecystectomy on Thursday. His last dialysis was Monday, and his potassium is 5.9 mEq/L with mild volume overload. What is the best preoperative step?
options: Dialyze the day before surgery to correct potassium and volume
Proceed to the operating room now and dialyze after the operation is finished
Give a large saline bolus to improve renal perfusion first
Hold dialysis until after surgery to avoid hypotension
items.explanation: Patients with end-stage renal disease should ideally be dialyzed within about 24 hours before elective or urgent surgery so that potassium, acid-base status, and volume are optimized, and uremic platelet dysfunction is reduced. Operating on a patient with hyperkalemia and overload risks arrhythmia and pulmonary edema. A saline bolus worsens overload in an anuric patient, and delaying dialysis until after surgery leaves the abnormalities uncorrected during anesthesia.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B with a Child-Pugh score of 12 and a hernia that is reducible and painless asks about elective repair. He has ascites and a bilirubin of 4.1 mg/dL. His model for end-stage liver disease score is 22. What is the best recommendation?
options: Proceed with open repair under general anesthesia at the next available operating room slot
Defer elective repair because operative mortality is very high at this stage
Proceed because hernia repair carries minimal risk in cirrhosis
Perform an immediate transjugular shunt to enable repair
items.explanation: Perioperative mortality rises steeply with the Child-Pugh score and model for end-stage liver disease score, and the highest Child-Pugh category carries a prohibitive risk for elective surgery. An asymptomatic reducible hernia can be observed, with optimization of ascites and consideration of transplant referral. Elective repair is not harmless in decompensated cirrhosis because of wound leak, infection, and hepatic failure. A shunt adds its own risk and does not justify elective repair.

items.stem: A surgical service is designing an enhanced recovery pathway for elective colorectal resection. Which of the following elements has the strongest supporting evidence?
options: Routine nasogastric decompression until bowel function returns
Fasting from midnight and routine mechanical bowel preparation alone
Early oral feeding and mobilization beginning on the day of surgery
Liberal intravenous fluids and prolonged bed rest for comfort
items.explanation: Enhanced recovery pathways combine preoperative counseling, limited fasting with carbohydrate loading, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, balanced fluid therapy, avoidance of routine tubes and drains, and early feeding and mobilization. Together they shorten stay and reduce complications. Routine nasogastric tubes, midnight fasting, bowel preparation without oral antibiotics, fluid excess, and prolonged bed rest have been shown to be unhelpful or harmful.

items.stem: An 85-year-old nursing home resident with a signed do-not-resuscitate order is brought in with a strangulated femoral hernia and needs emergency operation. She is lucid and agrees to surgery. How should her resuscitation status be handled?
options: Automatically suspend the order because anesthesia requires full resuscitation measures
Automatically cancel the surgery because of the order
Ignore the order since it was written in a different facility
Review the order with her, and document a negotiated plan for the perioperative period
items.explanation: A do-not-resuscitate order does not by itself preclude surgery. Required reconsideration means the patient or surrogate and the team discuss which interventions, such as intubation, vasopressors, or compressions, will be accepted during and after the operation, and the agreed plan is documented. Automatic suspension and automatic refusal both disregard patient autonomy, and orders from another facility remain evidence of her wishes.
